full_text:
For years, best ball players have operated under the assumption that deep threats are more deserving of a draft-day premium because of their superior ability to churn out high-ceiling weeks. It turns out that thinking is wrong — __WRs who run more short routes are the ones putting up the bigger weeks.__

WRs with a more shallow route tree (at least 45% of their routes coming short) average more FPG than deep threats (at least 25% of their routes coming deep). __By Half-PPR scoring (used throughout this article), the short group averages 11.5 FPG, while the deep threats average just 8.7 FPG____.__

In this article, we’ll look deeper into this counterintuitive finding to extract actionable takeaways for 2026 fantasy football, including targets and fades across managed redraft, best ball, and DFS formats.

Our Methodology
---------------

Using *Fantasy Points Data*, I observed 4,961 individual WR weeks from 2022-2025 (min. 60% route share in that week). Tight ends were not included in this study.

Some quick definitions on terms I’ll be using:

+ __Deep routes:__ Go routes and all other routes that have a depth of 20+ yards from the LOS

+ __Intermediate routes:__ routes with a depth between 10-19 yards from the LOS
+ __Short routes:__ routes with a depth under 10 yards, including behind the LOS
+ __Route Depth Mix:__ the % share of short vs intermediate vs deep routes

For each week and season, I bucketed route distribution into short, intermediate, and deep shares. Nothing major came of intermediate share on its own, so we’re focusing on short vs deep for most of this article.

For this study, “short,” “intermediate,” or “deep” routes are determined by the actual route depth (where the break occurs), measured by the *Fantasy Points Data* team. But, conceptually, you can classify slants, flats, crossers, and screens as always being in the short bucket alongside, occasionally, some shorter outs, digs, and hitches.

Deep routes are a bit more complicated, as they take small percentages across many routes — hitches, digs, outs, corners, and posts — but I’m also assigning vertical routes without breaks like go routes and seams to the deep bucket.

Additionally, you’ll notice that I have set a threshold for this argument of at least 45% of players' routes coming short and/or at least 25% of routes coming deep — these are where the natural cutpoints are, and you start to see meaningful FPG impacts for players. It still holds that you want a player to run more short and less deep at different thresholds, but these are where the numbers really start to separate.

Deep Scores Less and Short Scores More
--------------------------------------

Let's bucket every WR season from our sample (2022-2025, min. 8 qualifying games at 60%+ route share) two different ways — by season short-route share and by season deep-route share — and look at what their qualifying weeks averaged on FPG.

As a WR's season deep share goes up, his weekly FPG goes down.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/684966d1c07025adf9b89c3a493b286041f6c498)

As his season short share goes up, his weekly FPG goes up.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/b9f74fbe03033ee314b228889a9076c66b2e5019)

__TLDR:__ The higher a receiver’s short rate is, the higher his season-long average FPG. The higher the receiver’s deep share, the lower his average FPG.

Target Rate Gets Cut In Half
----------------------------

Why does FPG trend downward as route trees get deeper? __Well, the Target Per Route Run rate (TPRR) goes from 27% to 12% on short routes compared to deep routes.__ QBs simply throw to deeper routes less often! And we see a similar effect for virtually every other per-route metric; downfield targets happen so infrequently that even yards per route run (YPRR) and fantasy points per route run (FP/RR) fall.

Does the term [“Sacrificial X”](https://x.com/MattHarmon_BYB/status/2053981927493820452?s=20) stand out to you with all that in mind? (Shoutout to [Matt Harmon](https://x.com/MattHarmon_BYB?s=20) for one of the best phrases in football.)

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/79bef2e0de610fd67f35cd32f6a2b0aea12ac708)

Note that the above chart includes every route for every WR bucketed into short, intermediate, and deep to determine the metrics above, so we have a very strong sample size for these per-route metrics. __Keep in mind it is on a PER ROUTE basis — obviously PER TARGET, deep is much better, but that’s what led best ball drafters astray in the first place: seeing those big 12-FP plays coming on a deep ball that tilt an entire matchup.__

__TLDR:__ Lower TPRR means fewer chances at Fantasy Points per Route. Even intermediate routes result in largely better per-route metrics, further amplifying our idea that deeper is worse and shorter is better.

Average Depth of Route and Outliers
-----------------------------------

Another way we can observe deep threats is by looking at Average Depth of Route (ADOR), which provides another signal of a player’s typical roles. Think of it as a weighted average of route depth mix.

We see a similar relationship between ADOR and FPG as before. Players with an ADOR above 12.0 average just 8.7 FPG, while those with an ADOR below 12.0 average 10.4 FPG.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/aa996220c39da6c1706f88e7c5ad4a7d1f0dbebb)

First, notice that most of the elite WRs we're drafting in the first few rounds (e.g., Ja'Marr Chase, Puka Nacua, Jaxon Smith-Njigba) have relatively shallow route trees/low ADORs. The sweet spot for fantasy production is between 8.0 and 11.0.

Being lower in ADOR is better than being higher, but the optimal range is ~8-11 yards. If you’re below 8, it’s usually a unique Deebo Samuel-esque role, and the sample sizes get small. (Khalil Shakir, Rashee Rice, and Malik Washington are the only qualifying players from 2025 who fit in this bucket.)

__TLDR:__ You typically don’t want players with a high ADOR, which indicates a deep route mix.

Short Depth Players Boom More and Bust Less
-------------------------------------------

Any DFS and best-ball players reading this are likely wondering how our short and deep receivers play out on a weekly basis. Conventional wisdom would suggest that while deep threats may be inconsistent, they have uniquely strong weekly upside.

But this turns out to be false! The favorability of the more shallow route tree (45%+ short) compared to the deep threat tree (25%+ deep) holds for both weekly upside and downside. __Players with shorter route trees boom more and bust less.__

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/9cd014e633753301de3889fc8342a30d9c49e163)

I’m sure there’s a theoretical limit to this; in our sample, the only player with an ADOR below 7 and short rate above 65% is Khalil Shakir in 2024 and 2025. He didn’t reach 20.0 fantasy points a single time over this span, so perhaps his outlierishly shallow route tree did limit his upside. But away from that polar extreme, it is generally “higher upside” to run a shorter route tree rather than a deeper route tree.

__TLDR:__ Shorter depth players boom or smash twice as often as deep threats. Deep threats also bust more!

Correlations and Caveats
------------------------

We should remember that our analysis so far has the benefit of hindsight. But the good news is that the correlation year-over-year for route depth mix (% of short, intermediate, and deep) is very high at 70%. Nearly the same holds true for ADOR, regardless of whether you change teams.

Of course, that means that *some* players do shift into different buckets. So we should make an effort to think through potential year-to-year role changes, but by and large, players “own” their route-depth mix. So we *can* use this lens to spot values and fades in advance.

There will also always be outliers and elite players. Tyreek Hill (the outlier of all outliers) had some elite fantasy seasons with a very deep route profile, and George Pickens ran a lot of deep routes in 2025. In these cases, we have to make judgment calls.

4 Shallow Route Tree Players to Target
--------------------------------------

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/01efc35f5e179f119755fffa6b7676a00c49e7fa)

##### __Garrett Wilson__, NYJ — ADP 38.5

Wilson sits in the ADOR sweet spot on the scatter plot *and* boasts a 45%+ short-route share for three years in a row. He hit useful weeks 57% of the time in 2025, the highest rate on the entire targets list. The Jets moved from Justin Fields to Geno Smith, a massive QB upgrade for fantasy purposes (and I’m not even a big Geno fan).

 It's almost impossible to overstate how significant the upgrade is from Justin Fields to Geno Smith from a fantasy perspective Worst QB Seasons by Completions per Dropback [2021-2025] 1. Anthony Richardson, 2024 (42%) 2. Justin Fields, 2022 (44%) 3. Justin Fields, 2021 (45%) 4.… pic.twitter.com/lD0VnTQKtE — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) June 10, 2026 

And remember, even with the combination of Justin Fields and Tyrod Taylor, Wilson averaged 15.7 FPG (~WR5) in the five games before he injured his knee last year.

##### __Luther Burden III__, CHI — ADP 41.8

This one is somewhat of a bet on Ben Johnson and a little leap on Luther Burden’s talent, but the environment became cleaner: D.J. Moore was traded to Buffalo, Olamide Zaccheaus signed with Atlanta, and Johnson already said [he is buying Burden stock](https://x.com/AdamSchefter/status/2060067106775871908?s=20). As a rookie, Burden was treated as a short-area player, but he was not on the field enough for season-long fantasy relevance (just 3 games of a 60%+ route share). Being a short-route player also protects him from Caleb Williams’ inaccuracies, which seemingly can only improve.

We’re betting on the profile (less deep, more short) and Burden inheriting the[](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2055320609748299941?s=20)[coveted slot role](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2055320609748299941?s=20) in Ben Johnson’s offense, in which Amon-Ra St. Brown averaged 15.1 FP/G for Johnson in 2024 on a near-identical route tree.

##### __Jaylen Waddle__, DEN — ADP 49.3

Only 6% of Waddle’s 2025 games landed in the 25%+ deep bucket, one of the lowest deep-heavy rates among all 60%+ route-share WRs. The trade to Denver puts him in a Sean Payton offense, and [early OTA reports](https://www.denverbroncos.com/news/annual-meeting-notebook-hc-sean-payton-highlights-strength-of-wr-jaylen-waddle-s-game-outlines-plan-for-voluntary-offseason-program) already frame Waddle as an inside/outside chess piece who immediately changes the offense. I believe he maintains the short-to-intermediate role, with Courtland Sutton continuing in his intermediate-to-deep profile.

That’s a bit of a projection, but Waddle was at a 50% short rate in 2023 and 47% in 2024 – he’s morphed into a short-area player. Admittedly, the sample size of players who switched teams in our data and had a significant enough role to matter is small. But within the sample, players have a strong correlation coefficient of 0.73 between the route-depth mix on their old and new teams.

Bo Nix is recovering from a broken ankle and recently practiced for the first time. Waddle's route tree is perfect for their quick passing game. It doesn’t hurt that he’s also a top ASS guy — he’s a clear buy.

##### __Rashee Rice__, KC — ADP 30.2

For Rice, my enthusiasm centers on his short-route rate, the way the Chiefs can scam him open, and some optimism about how the offense could operate slightly differently with Eric Bieniemy inserted as offensive coordinator instead of Matt Nagy.

Rashee has the most extreme short profile among the top-100 WRs by ADP. He did not have a single game in which he ran 25%+ of his routes deep, and we know how sticky roles are year-to-year from earlier. In 2025, Patrick Mahomes averaged 22.3 ATT/G within 9 yards of the LOS, and Rice runs 62% of his routes inside that depth. In an 8-game 2025 sample, Rice hit useful weeks 50% of the time and spike weeks 50% of the time — the highest spike rate of any target on this list.

The off-field risk is real — he could do something to go back to jail or receive a suspension literally any day — but he’s out and should be healthy for training camp. Our takeaway from this study is that his short route depth is not a downside, but a boon to his fantasy prospects.

4 Deep Threats to Fade
----------------------

These players either qualify under the 12+ ADOR OR 25%+ deep route share bucket:

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/d494dc97501adcc7c4b565ea1b92083b739e3c25)

##### __Jordan Addison__, MIN — ADP 86.3

Addison is squarely in the 12+ ADOR zone, which, coupled with a sub-20% TPRR, is brutal for fantasy__.__ His career useful-rate (10+ fantasy points) trajectory is 44% (2023) → 33% (2024) → 14% (2025), with spike rates (15+ fantasy points) going from 12% → 13% → __0%__. He didn’t earn a single top-12 weekly WR finish in 2025. While his brutal 2025 owes in part to JJ McCarthy’s struggles, Addison’s spike rates were still low in 2023 and 2024, when he had much better QB play.

Addison has no opportunity to displace Justin Jefferson as the alpha. The offense also added another short-to-intermediate threat in Jauan Jennings, further securing Addison’s deep-threat role that could push his deep rate up. Kyler Murray also sits below the league average on % of pass attempts 20+ yards down the field in our charted data. There are too many reasons to fade.

##### __Courtland Sutton__, DEN — ADP 80.8

Sutton’s 12.28 ADOR could get deeper in 2026. He hit useful weeks 41% of the time in 2025, but spike weeks only 12% of the time. That’s below many WRs currently being drafted around him (DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman Jr., Chris Godwin Jr., and Quentin Johnston), even when he had the benefit of being the Broncos’ clear WR1. Then Denver traded for Waddle, who immediately adds the separation and underneath juice this offense was missing.

In Sean Payton’s offenses, there’s always been an underneath guy and a deep guy. They’ve gone deep-guy-by-committee for a few seasons with Marvin Mims, Troy Franklin, and Courtland Sutton. But Sutton also filled in by doing some short and intermediate work as the team’s WR1. Now they have their short-area star in Jaylen Waddle to draw Sutton’s TPRR down and move his route tree deeper. Add in some aging risk (Sutton turns 31 years old this October, an age at which production [often starts to fall off](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/age-curves-when-nfl-players-break-out#/)) and that he goes in the same round as upside QB bets like Justin Herbert and Trevor Lawrence, and I don’t see much upside for the opportunity cost.

##### __Alec Pierce__, IND — ADP 73.4

On top of the metrics above, Pierce also had an absurd 19.4 ADoT — 5.1 yards deeper than any other WR in the NFL with a 60% route share. He’s been the purest deep-tree WR in football, averaging below a 25% short rate and above a 25% deep rate every year of his career. His performance across a large sample of short routes is also 38% worse than the average WR performs on short routes.

Pierce’s career useful (10+ FP) rates are 6% (2023), 31% (2024), and 33% (2025), with boom (20+ FP) rates of 0%, 20%, and 13%. His ADP has now jumped from WR60+ all three prior seasons to WR36 in 2026, a 100+ pick rise. There’s either a ton of projection happening around what the loss of Michael Pittman Jr. means for his role (fewer deep routes), or a misconception that his profile is spikier than it is.

The general fantasy football player assigns a “spikey” profile to Pierce, even though that’s not what our data tells us (for example, a hobbled Chris Godwin Jr. had a slightly higher boom rate at 14% and goes after Alec Pierce with a nicer route profile). Pierce hits on all archetype red flags (12+ ADOR and 25%+ deep rate). Add in the uncertainty with his ankle, and he’s an easy fade for me.

##### __Brian Thomas Jr.__, JAX — ADP 63.6

After Jacksonville's 2025 usage shift (beginning in Week 13, when Jakobi Meyers played his first game), Thomas ran over 30% of his routes deep and landed in the 25%+ deep bucket in 5 of 6 games. His aDOT also skyrocketed to 18.1 in that time period, nearly as high as Alec Pierce’s.

Thomas’s 2024 (53% useful rate, 24% spike rate, with a varied route depth mix) and 2025 (deep route tree, 14% useful rate, 7% spike rate) made him two completely different fantasy players. [And it continues to sound like BTJ will be used in a similar role to the end of last season](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2061495165848621381?s=20).

Until Liam Coen says something that suggests Thomas won’t be living in the 25%+ deep route zone, I have him as a fade.

\> __Note:__ I excluded Quentin Johnston and Jameson Williams from this list, even though they meet the criteria. Based on[](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2065893813172736210?s=20)[reports](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2065893813172736210?s=20), I expect Johnston to have a shorter route tree in 2026. Jameson Williams has a major playcaller change, which creates more ambiguity than I felt comfortable with.

3 Values Outside the Top 100
----------------------------

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/749f7f06e880789c201279a0ca4c6aaa14d94a08/ad6119681676304c8198b309fc8ad068a18b9c84)

##### __Wan'Dale Robinson__, TEN — ADP 116.6

Robinson just posted his first 1,000-yard season for the Giants (92 catches, 1,014 yards), then signed a 4-year, $78M deal with Tennessee to reunite with Brian Daboll, now the Titans' offensive coordinator. Daboll already built him into a top-20 WR in his short-area role in New York. Staying short insulates him from some of Cam Ward’s inaccuracies, unlike what I presume Carnell Tate’s role might be.

The contract matters because it suggests intent; Daboll got Robinson paid to do what he did in New York. He goes in an area where other guys typically project for ~600-700 receiving yards, and that seems like his floor based on his profile.

##### __Stefon Diggs__, FA — ADP 132.8

Diggs hit useful weeks at a 67% rate, and spike weeks at a 33% rate in the 12 games where he ran 60% or more of the routes — those numbers are pretty much in line with Chris Olave, who goes in Round 3. Diggs has been a 50%+ short-route guy for most of his career, and his 2025 sample with New England looked the same. The Patriots released him in March, and he remains unsigned as of this writing. His only downfall last year was his route share (partly because of his brutal knee injury in 2024).

If he signs anywhere with a functional passing offense, a 132.8 ADP is a steal.

##### __Ryan Flournoy__, DAL — ADP 170.2

This is more in the dart throw range, but Flournoy’s route depth and TPRR (0.21 in 2025, ahead of Brian Thomas and Marvin Harrison Jr.) profile is very strong for his ADP. Flournoy is locked in as the Cowboys’ WR3, but is one of the few true fantasy football WR handcuffs if CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens misses time. Flournoy averaged 9.8 FPG (~WR27) across five games in which Lamb was inactive in 2025, hitting 15.0+ fantasy points twice in that span.

Many notable analysts view Flournoy as a breakout talent (including me), and the route profile shows it’s possible. Flournoy operates shorter, while Pickens goes deeper, with Lamb in the intermediate area. He hits all of the thresholds pretty cleanly, so it’s the right dart throw at a pretty inexpensive cost.
